title: Special methods
lesson:
Make a class and print one of its objects, and you get something like `<__main__.Harvest object at 0x7f3a...>`. Compare two objects with the same data using `==` and you get `False`. Try `sorted()` on a list of them and Python stops with a TypeError. Your objects don't yet know how to act like normal Python values.

**Special methods** (also called dunder methods, for the double underscores) fix that. You never call them yourself: Python calls them when you use the normal syntax.

- `__str__(self)`: what `print(obj)` and `str(obj)` show. Write it for people: `Amina: 40 kg maize`.
- `__repr__(self)`: what you see in the shell, in a printed list and in error messages. Write it for programmers, ideally so it looks like the code that would rebuild the object: `Harvest('Amina', 'maize', 40)`. Use `{self.farmer!r}` in an f-string to get the quotes right.
- `__eq__(self, other)`: what `==` means. Without it, `==` only checks "is this the very same object".
- `__lt__(self, other)`: what `<` means. `sorted()`, `min()` and `max()` all use `<`, so defining it makes your objects sortable.

```
def __eq__(self, other):
    if not isinstance(other, Harvest):
        return NotImplemented
    return self.farmer == other.farmer and self.kg == other.kg

def __lt__(self, other):
    if not isinstance(other, Harvest):
        return NotImplemented
    return self.kg < other.kg
```

`NotImplemented` is a special value that tells Python "I don't know how to compare with that". Python then tries the other side, and falls back to `False` for `==` or a clear TypeError for `<`. That's better than crashing with an AttributeError deep inside your method.

**Common mistakes**
- `__str__` must **return** a string. Printing inside it and returning nothing gives "TypeError: __str__ returned non-string".
- Defining `__eq__` makes the object unhashable (you can't use it as a dict key or in a set) unless you also write `__hash__`. Next unit's dataclasses can handle that for you.
- One class, many possible orders? Give `__lt__` the natural one, and use `sorted(items, key=lambda h: h.farmer)` for the others.

**In real programs** a good `__repr__` makes debugging fast: when a list of 50 enemies prints as `[Slime(hp=4), Skeleton(hp=10), ...]` you see the problem at a glance. Leaderboards, task queues and "closest enemy first" targeting all rely on objects that compare.

notes: __str__ is the friendly text print() uses.
__repr__ looks like code; !r adds the quotes around text.
__eq__ compares the data, and says NotImplemented for other types.
__lt__ by kg is all sorted(), min() and max() need.
A printed list uses __repr__ for each item.

exercises.title: A printable harvest
exercises.prompt:
Class Harvest(farmer, crop, kg) is started for you. Add:
- __str__: returns like Amina: 40 kg maize
- __repr__: returns like Harvest('Amina', 'maize', 40), so that it looks like the code that would build the same object (use !r in the f-string).

tests.check:
h = Harvest("O'Neil", 'maize', 3)
back = eval(repr(h), {'Harvest': Harvest})
assert (back.farmer, back.crop, back.kg) == ("O'Neil", 'maize', 3), 'repr should rebuild the same harvest, even with a quote in the name: use !r'
tests.name: repr rebuilds the object
tests.hint_if_fail: Write {self.farmer!r} instead of '{self.farmer}': !r picks the right quotes for you.

hints: Both methods must return a string, not print it.

exercises.title: Equal and sortable
exercises.prompt:
Class Harvest(farmer, kg). Add:
- __eq__: two harvests are equal when farmer AND kg are the same. Comparing with something that isn't a Harvest returns NotImplemented (so == gives False).
- __lt__: a harvest is less than another when its kg is smaller (so sorted() goes from smallest to biggest). Non-Harvest: return NotImplemented.
- __repr__ is given.

tests.check:
assert Harvest('Amina', 40) == Harvest('Amina', 40), 'same farmer and kg should be equal'
assert not (Harvest('Amina', 40) == Harvest('Amina', 41)), 'different kg: not equal'
assert Harvest('Amina', 40) != Harvest('Juma', 40), 'different farmer: not equal'
tests.name: equality

tests.check:
hs = [Harvest('Amina', 40), Harvest('Juma', 12), Harvest('Wanjiru', 55), Harvest('Otieno', 30)]
got = [h.farmer for h in sorted(hs)]
assert got == ['Juma', 'Otieno', 'Amina', 'Wanjiru'], 'sorted order was %r' % got
tests.name: sorted by kg

tests.check:
h = Harvest('Amina', 40)
assert (h == 'Amina') is False, 'comparing with a string should just be False'
assert Harvest('Amina', 40) in [Harvest('Juma', 1), Harvest('Amina', 40)], '`in` uses ==: an equal harvest should be found'
tests.name: other types and `in`
tests.hint_if_fail: Start both methods with: if not isinstance(other, Harvest): return NotImplemented

tests.name: < with a number

hints: Both methods return True or False (or NotImplemented).
First line of each: if not isinstance(other, Harvest): return NotImplemented
__eq__: return self.farmer == other.farmer and self.kg == other.kg. __lt__: return self.kg < other.kg

exercises.title: A game leaderboard
exercises.prompt:
Class Score(player, points, seconds) for a game. Add:
- __str__: like Juma 120 (45s)
- __lt__: a score comes BEFORE another (is "less") when it has MORE points; with equal points, the FASTER time (fewer seconds) comes first. So sorted() puts the best score first.
- leaderboard(scores): a function (not a method) that returns a list of the str() of each score, best first. An empty list gives [].

tests.name: tie: faster first
tests.hint_if_fail: When the points are equal, compare seconds: fewer seconds comes first.

hints: sorted() puts the 'smallest' first. Here 'smallest' must mean 'best', so __lt__ returns True when self has MORE points.
if self.points != other.points: return self.points > other.points
Otherwise return self.seconds < other.seconds. leaderboard is [str(s) for s in sorted(scores)].

quiz.q: You print an object whose class has no __str__ or __repr__. What do you see?
quiz.why: The default only shows the class and memory address.

quiz.q: Which special method does sorted() need on your objects?
Your class has no __eq__. a = Harvest('A', 1); b = Harvest('A', 1). What is a == b?
quiz.why: Without __eq__, == only checks if they are the very same object.

quiz.q: Why return NotImplemented instead of False from __lt__ when other isn't a Harvest?
choices: Python can try the other side, then give a clear TypeError
quiz.why: NotImplemented lets Python handle mixed types properly.
Containers show their items with repr.

cards.a: __str__ is friendly text for print; __repr__ is for programmers and looks like code.

cards.q: What does !r do in an f-string?
cards.a: Uses repr(), so text gets its quotes.

cards.q: What should __eq__ return for an unrelated type?

explain: Explain what __repr__ is for and why it helps when you debug, with an example object you make up.
